subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram‑negative diplococcus that can rapidly cause meningitis or septicemia, especially in adolescents and young adults. Early recognition and prompt treatment are lifesaving.

sections.p: N. meningitidis is a small, oxidase‑positive diplococcus that lives in the nasopharynx. It can invade the bloodstream and central nervous system, producing meningitis or meningococcemia.
b: Encapsulated, polysaccharide capsule is main virulence factor
Capsule types A, B, C, W, Y

sections.p: The capsule protects against phagocytosis and complement. Pili and opacity proteins aid adhesion to mucosal cells.
b: Opacity protein Opa for immune evasion

sections.p: Transmission is via respiratory droplets. Colonisation is asymptomatic; invasive disease occurs when the bacterium breaches mucosal barriers.
Acute meningitis and meningococcemia with petechial rash. Rapid progression can lead to shock, DIC, and adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse‑Friderichsen).
b: Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status

sections.p: Clinical suspicion plus rapid laboratory tests. CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein. Blood cultures and PCR confirm.

t.b: Neutrophilic pleocytosis indicates bacterial meningitis; high WBC >1000/mm3 suggests severe infection
Elevated (>100 mg/dL) reflects blood‑brain barrier disruption
Positive in ~70% of meningococcemia cases; identifies serogroup
Rapid, high sensitivity; useful when antibiotics already started

sections.p: Empiric therapy with third‑generation cephalosporin plus doxycycline or rifampicin for contacts. Supportive care for shock and DIC. Vaccination prevents most serogroups.
b: Cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) chosen for CNS penetration and low resistance

t.b: Used for post‑exposure prophylaxis; oral route convenient in low‑resource settings
Effective prophylaxis; avoid in patients with liver disease or drug interactions

sections.p: Remember the classic triad of meningitis and the rapid progression to shock. Waterhouse‑Friderichsen is a medical emergency. Vaccination coverage gaps explain outbreaks.
b: Waterhouse‑Friderichsen: adrenal hemorrhage causes sudden death

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening headache, neck stiffness, fever, petechial rash, confusion, or shock

faq.a: Yes, conjugate vaccines cover serogroups A, C, W, Y, and B in many countries. Routine childhood and adolescent immunisation reduces outbreaks.

faq.q: What if a patient has already started antibiotics?
faq.a: PCR and antigen tests remain useful; blood cultures may be negative. Clinical diagnosis still guides treatment.

faq.q: Why is a third‑generation cephalosporin preferred?
faq.a: It penetrates the CSF well, has broad activity against N. meningitidis, and has a favourable safety profile in children and adults.

exam: Explain why a patient with sudden onset fever, neck stiffness, and petechial rash should be treated immediately for meningococcemia.
Describe the pathophysiology of Waterhouse‑Friderichsen syndrome and its clinical implications.
Outline the steps of post‑exposure prophylaxis for close contacts of a meningococcal case.
